description: Minesweeper online free: the classic minefield in your browser. Reveal every safe cell, flag the mines, and clear the board without setting one off.
lede: The classic minefield, exactly as you remember it. A grid of covered cells hides a fixed number of mines, and every number you uncover tells you how many mines touch that cell. Work out where they are, flag them, and reveal everything else — one wrong tap ends the round. It starts on a friendly 9×9 board with 10 mines, and the expert board hides 99 mines in 480 cells.

p: Tap a cell to reveal it. Your first tap is always safe — the mines are only placed after it, away from that cell and its neighbours. If the cell is empty, the whole empty area around it opens at once. If it has a number, that number counts the mines touching it, including diagonally.

Use the numbers to work out where the mines are. When you are sure a cell hides a mine, flag it: long-press it on a phone, right-click it on a computer, or turn on the flag button at the top and tap it. Reveal every safe cell to win. Tap a mine and the round is over.

A 1 in a corner leaves only three suspects, so corners are the easiest place to start reasoning. When a 1 touches exactly one covered cell, that cell is a mine; when it touches no covered cells besides the ones you already flagged, every other neighbour is safe.

Chording speeds everything up: tap a revealed number whose flags already match it, and all its other covered neighbours open at once. It is the fastest way to clear a board, and the most common way to blow one up, so only chord when you have counted twice.

sections.h: A game from the Windows era
p: Minesweeper became famous as a pack-in with Microsoft Windows, first appearing in the Windows 3.1 Entertainment Pack in 1990, written by Robert Donner and Curt Johnson. It was not the first of its kind — mine-hunting games ran on mainframes in the 1960s and 70s — but the Windows version put it on millions of office desks, where it quietly became one of the most played puzzle games in history.

The game has a devoted speedrunning scene: expert players clear the 30×16 board in under 40 seconds, and the world record sits in the low thirties. Most players never get near that, and that is fine — a careful beginner clear is its own small triumph.

ol: Start in a corner or an edge. Fewer neighbours means fewer suspects, and a 1 there often solves itself.
Flag as you go. Every flag you place turns the numbers around it into simpler sums, and the mine counter at the top tells you how many are left.
When two numbers share neighbours, subtract. If a 2 and a 1 overlap, the extra mine must be in the cells only the 2 touches.
Never guess while a safe move exists. Scan the whole board first — there is almost always one more deduction hiding somewhere.
When you truly have to guess, pick the cell whose neighbours give you the most information either way, and keep the 50/50 coin flips for last.

p: For another numbers puzzle with no luck involved, slide the tiles in [[2048]] or match the pairs in [[memory-match]]. If you would rather test your reactions, try the [[reaction-time-test]] or whack moles in [[whack-a-mole]]. You can find every old favourite among the [[cat:classic|classic games]] and [[cat:puzzle|puzzle games]].

faq: Is my first click always safe?
Yes. The mines are only placed after your first tap, and never on that cell or any of its neighbours, so the first reveal can never be a mine.
How do I flag a mine on a phone?
Long-press the cell, or tap the flag button at the top and then tap cells to flag them. Tap the flag button again to go back to revealing.
What does the number on a cell mean?
It counts the mines in the eight cells around it, including diagonally. A 1 means exactly one of its neighbours is a mine.
Reveal every cell that is not a mine. You do not have to flag every mine to win, but flagging helps you keep track — and your best time is saved per difficulty.
